title: Paired texts: how a displaced sculpin finds its pool
bodyMd:
**Text 1**

Tide-pool sculpins carried away from their home pool and released as far as a hundred metres down the shore often return within a single tide cycle. Marine biologist Tomás Herrera argues that the fish memorise the shape of the shore at high water, when the pools are joined and a sculpin can swim freely above them. On his account, the return trip is navigation from a remembered map.

**Text 2**

Biologist Ingrid Vogel doubts that a map is needed. In her flume experiments, sculpins swam steadily toward water carrying the scent of the algae and invertebrates of their own pool, even though the flume offered no landmarks at all. Vogel grants that displaced sculpins do get home; she holds that they may simply be swimming up a chemical gradient rather than consulting a memory.
accessibilityText: Two short related passages. Text 1: tide-pool sculpins released up to a hundred metres from their home pool often return within one tide cycle. Marine biologist Tomas Herrera argues the fish memorise the shape of the shore at high water, when the pools join and a sculpin can swim above them, so the return is navigation from a remembered map. Text 2: biologist Ingrid Vogel doubts a map is needed. In her flume experiments sculpins swam steadily toward water carrying the scent of their own pool's algae and invertebrates, even with no landmarks present. Vogel accepts that displaced sculpins do return home, but says they may simply swim up a chemical gradient rather than use a memory.

provenance.notes: Original paired texts written for this item bank. Both researchers, the flume experiment and the hundred-metre displacement are invented; homing in intertidal fish is used only as general background.
